newsitem.title: UK: EU Social Chapter fears may be more imagined than real.
newsitem.headline: EU Social Chapter fears may be more imagined than real.

text.p: Many British business leaders will have winced on Monday at news that the new minister for Europe, Doug Henderson, is flying to Brussels to start the process of joining the European Union Social Chapter immediately.

Businessmen fear the Social Chapter, a framework for laws guaranteeing employment rights, will cut competitiveness and cost jobs, particularly if it is introduced in conjunction with a national minimum wage -- another Labour pledge.
But so far the Social Chapter boasts only two, inoffensive pieces of legislation, allowing unpaid leave for new parents, and some consultation rights for workers' councils.

The Chapter gives all working parents the right to three months' unpaid leave after the birth of their child and says employees in multi-national firms have the right to be informed of corporate changes through works councils.
Still, the sceptics say, the real problem is the Social Chapter framework could be the gateway to a flood of further legislation in the future.
But given that the Chapter has been in existence for five years, and still boasts only two laws, there appears to be little rush to set up a whole swathe of new regulations.
And in any case, supporters say the Labour government's policy is to retain a veto over new laws in key areas.

On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Robin Cook proclaimed the government's intention to sign the Chapter as soon as possible. "We do not think that the British people should be second class citizens with less rights than employees on the continent."
But he added the government would retain its veto on social security issues as well as external border controls.

Adair Turner, director-general of the Confederation of British Industry, said the veto would cut the risk of damaging laws being drafted. "Labour's commitment to maintain the veto...is welcome and limits the risks of harmful measures," he wrote in Monday's Financial Times.

A recent Reuter poll of directors of 20 leading British companies found an even split over the Social Chapter. Ten said the chapter would have a fairly negative or a very negative impact on business. The rest said it would not affect them.

After the scale of Labour's landslide election win became apparent on Friday, business groups rushed to congratulate Tony Blair's party. But they also quickly demanded clarification on workplace policies like the Social Chapter.
The British Chambers of Commerce flatly called for Britain's opt-out to be maintained. The BCC represents smaller firms which may find it harder to bear the costs of the Social Chapter.

But the CBI, Britain's top employers group, was far less damning. "The Social Chapter makes it vital that Mr Blair delivers on his promise to campaign for flexible labour markets in Europe -- and that he succeeds," Turner said.
A by-product of adopting the Social Chapter is that it could signal an era of better British relations with the EU -- vital given that 60 percent of British trade is with Europe.

Many top businessmen backed ousted Prime Minister John Major's refusal to sign the Social Chapter, on the grounds that Britain's flexible labour market laws were a key factor behind its economic recovery.

But even the most fearful would be hard pushed to swallow the Conservatives' contention that it would cost 500,000 jobs. And by the time of the election, many felt the antagonistic rhetoric of Eurosceptic Conservatives was harming Britain's position in Europe. In a letter to the Financial Times in March, Sir Colin Marshall, president of the CBI and chairman of British Airways Plc, and 22 other top businessmen, slammed Euroscepticism. To alienate Britain's major trading partners was folly, they said.

"These benefits would be put at risk if this country chose the path of isolation," the letter said. "Britain would be a poorer place, with lower investment and higher unemployment." In that respect, Labour's pledge to complete the EU single market, allowing British companies open access to all corners of Europe will be music to their ears, and more important than any dangers posed by the Social Chapter.
"The completion of the single market is vitally important for business," Turner said on Monday. "The government's intention to make it a priority...is very welcome."
